newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open higher, jobless claims ahead.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open higher, jobless claims ahead.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries opened higher on Thursday, following strength in Europe overnight and in front of the weekly U.S. report on new jobless claims.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year Treasury bond was up 8/32 to 99-3/32, yielding 6.82 percent, in early trade. The bond yield pushed through resistance at 6.85 percent, closing at 6.84 percent on Wednesday.
The two-year Treasury note was up 1/32 to 100-2/32, yielding 5.97 percent.
Jobless claims for the week ended September 28, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, are expected to total 341,000, barely changed from last week's 340,000.

The only other economic report the market will get is August factory orders, due at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT. Economists surveyed by Reuters estimated, on average, that factory orders fell 1.2 percent in August after rising 1.8 percent in July.

Data like those would do nothing to cloud the market's currently sunny disposition. The same is true of the key U.S. September employment report due Friday if it comes in as expected with more subdued payroll growth of 165,000 new jobs.

"The market's been in a better frame of mind ever since the Fed stayed on hold," said Kim Rupert, senior economist at MMS International, referring to the Federal Reserve's decision last week to keep interest rates steady.
Rupert said the market's close Wednesday above some resistance levels and expectations of a "relatively friendly employment report" on Friday were providing momentum.
"Eurodebt markets were up overnight and continue to support us," Rupert added. "And the dollar has also been on the firmer side though we saw a little bit of profit-taking in Japan last night."
Rupert said the jobless cliams report at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT "shouldn't be too much of a problem.
"The market is looking for basically an unchanged number," she said. "So unless we get a surprise on the downside on the claims number, the market will stay fairly well bid."

Because the market already got the August report on durable goods, with a decline of 3.1 percent, economists are confident that "there's going to be a big decline" in the August factory orders report.
"That's not much of a market mover and especially not before payrolls tomorrrow," said Rupert.
